titleStmt.title: Adapting the Interface, Not the Model: Runtime Harness Adaptation for Deterministic LLM Agents

analytic.title: Adapting the Interface, Not the Model: Runtime Harness Adaptation for Deterministic LLM Agents

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

keywords.term: Parameter Adaptation Runtime Interface Adaptation Training trajectories

div.p: LLM agents are shaped not only by their language models, but also by the runtime harness that mediates observation, tool use, action execution, feedback interpretation, and trajectory control. While existing agent adaptation methods mainly update model parameters, many failures in deterministic, rulegoverned domains stem from mismatches at the model-environment interface. We propose LIFE-HARNESS, a lifecycle-aware runtime harness that improves frozen LLM agents without changing model weights or evaluation environments. LIFE-HARNESS evolves from training trajectories by converting recurring interaction failures into reusable interventions across environment contracts, procedural skills, action realization, and trajectory regulation, and remains fixed for evaluation on unseen tasks. We evaluate LIFE-HARNESS across eight environments from AgentBench, τ -bench, τ 2 -bench, and Ap-pWorld using 18 open-weight backbones, and further test three frontier models on seven environments. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct, LIFE-HARNESS exceeds Meta-Harness and AHE by 28.7 and 7.5 percentage points in mean accuracy across the seven shared environments, respectively, while using 8.5% and 68.4% fewer optimization tokens. The evolved harnesses also benefit GPT 5.5, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, yielding an average accuracy gain of 3.5 percentage points. Code is available at GitHub.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: An LLM agent is not just an LLM. As shown in Figure 2 (a), it is a model embedded in a stateful interaction loop: the environment exposes observations, the runtime system specifies available tools and actions, the model emits an action or tool call, an executor applies it to the environment, and the resulting feedback updates the next decision (Wang et al., 2024;Anthropic, 2026). The resulting behavior is therefore determined not only by the model, but also by the runtime harness that mediates how the model observes the environment, understands tools, realizes actions, and interprets feedback. This system-level view is increasingly important across agent applications, including software engineering assistants (Yang et al., 2024b;OpenAI, 2026;OpenCode, 2026), web navigation (Zhou et al., 2024), database manipulation (Lei et al., 2025), operating-system control (Xie et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2024), tool-using business workflow agents (Yao et al., 2024;Barres et al., 2025), and embodied interaction (Shridhar et al., 2020). Despite this, agent adaptation is commonly framed as model adaptation, including model scaling (Grattafiori et al., 2024;Qwen Team et al., 2025), fine-tuning (Chen et al., 2023;Prabhakar et al., 2025), reinforcement learning (Guo et al., 2025;Qi et al., 2025), and distillation (Kang et al., 2025;Agarwal et al., 2024b). These approaches are powerful but implicitly absorb domain-specific behavior into model parameters. In deterministic, rule-governed domains, much of the relevant structure instead lives outside the model: tool schemas, API contracts, admissible actions,

div.head: Fixed & reusable across models
div.p: Figure 2: (a) An agent is not just an LLM: its behavior is shaped by the runtime harness that mediates observations, tools, actions, and feedback. (b) We adapt this runtime interface, rather than model parameters, yielding a fixed and reusable harness for frozen agents across deterministic environments. feedback rules, stopping conditions, and recovery strategies. This distinction is reflected in the gap between static capability and interactive performance. For example, Qwen3.5-4B achieves 74.0% on HMMT Feb (Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament, 2026), a competition-level mathematical reasoning benchmark, but only 43.1% on ALF-World (Shridhar et al., 2020), a deterministic embodied interaction benchmark. Such failures often arise from model-environment mismatches rather than limited reasoning ability. These include poorly structured observations, misunderstood tool contracts, non-executable actions, feedback that fails to trigger recovery, or degenerate trajectory dynamics. As illustrated in Figure 2 (b), this suggests another route to improvement: exposing stable environment-side structure via the runtime interface where the model observes, acts, and recovers.

Recent work has explored runtime harness optimization for frozen LLM agents, including reasoning-time compute control for mathematical reasoning (Zheng et al., 2026), online workspace adaptation in interactive games (Sarafian et al., 2026;Karten et al., 2026), harness-flag tuning (Sengupta and Wang, 2026), and automated harnesscode search (Lee et al., 2026;Lin et al., 2026). While these approaches show promise for harness optimization, their applicability and efficiency remain limited: some target specific domains or predefined configuration spaces, while broader codelevel search can incur substantial optimization costs without explicitly leveraging the structure of recurring interaction failures. We instead focus on deterministic agent domains, where the harness serves as a stable runtime interface between a frozen model and a rule-governed environment. In this setting, recurring failures can be localized to specific stages of the interaction lifecycle, allowing us to evolve failure-specific interface interventions from train-ing trajectories and then fix them during evaluation on unseen tasks. This raises our central question: Can training trajectories reveal stable failure structures that can be converted into a structured runtime interface to improve LLM agents across unseen tasks and diverse model architectures?

We answer this question with LIFE-HARNESS, a lifecycle-aware runtime harness for deterministic LLM agents. Rather than updating model parameters or searching over unconstrained harness code (Lee et al., 2026;Lin et al., 2026), LIFE-HARNESS adapts the runtime layer that mediates how a frozen model observes the environment, uses tools, realizes actions, interprets feedback, and recovers from degenerate trajectories. To model this runtime interface, LIFE-HARNESS organizes adaptation into four lifecycle layers. The Environment Contract Layer calibrates tool descriptions and interface constraints before interaction. The Procedural Skill Layer distills reusable procedures from trajectories and retrieves them for the current task and state. The Action Realization Layer validates and canonicalizes model-generated actions before execution, preventing deterministic failures. The Trajectory Regulation Layer monitors post-execution dynamics, detects degenerate patterns such as repetition, stagnation, invalid retries, or budget exhaustion, and triggers recovery when needed.

LIFE-HARNESS evolves through an iterative cycle in which an evolution LLM diagnoses recurring failures in training trajectories and proposes targeted updates to the four runtime layers. Each candidate is validated and compared with the current harness on the same training batch, and retained only if accuracy improves. The selected harness is then frozen for evaluation on unseen tasks.

We evaluate LIFE-HARNESS on eight agent environments from AgentBench (Liu et al., 2024), τ -bench (Yao et al., 2024), τ 2 -bench (Barres et al., 2025), and AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024). With Qwen3-4B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025), LIFE-HARNESS achieves a mean accuracy of 64.45% across the seven AgentBench and τ environments, exceeding Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) and AHE (Lin et al., 2026) by 28.7 and 7.5 percentage points (pp), respectively. It uses 8.5% fewer evolution tokens than Meta-Harness and 68.4% fewer than AHE. The harnesses evolved with Qwen3-4B-Instruct are reused across the other 17 instructiontuned, reasoning, and agent-specialized backbones, improving 132 of 144 model-environment settings across all eight environments. On AppWorld, mean accuracy improves by 5.3 pp. The evolved harnesses also benefit frontier models on the seven AgentBench and τ environments, yielding mean accuracy gains of 2.8, 4.4, and 3.4 pp for GPT 5.5, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, respectively.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) We formulate harness-based runtime interface adaptation for deterministic LLM agents, framing agent improvement as evolving the reusable interface between a frozen model and a rule-governed environment. (2) We introduce LIFE-HARNESS, a lifecycle-aware framework that converts recurring trajectory failures into targeted interventions across environment contracts, procedural skills, action realization, and trajectory regulation. (3) We demonstrate crossmodel effectiveness across eight environments and 18 backbones, and establish higher mean accuracy than Meta-Harness and AHE with lower evolution token budgets. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness and reusability of structured runtime interface adaptation.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Harness Optimization. Prior work adapts agent architectures, workflows, and environment interfaces. ADAS (Hu et al., 2025) and AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025) optimize architectures and workflows, while WALL-E (Zhou et al., 2025) learns environment rules for planning. Closer to runtime interaction, ALIGN (Liu et al., 2025) generates environment interfaces, and AgentSquare (Shang et al., 2025) searches modular agent architectures. Recent work further optimizes runtime scaffolds around frozen LLMs (Zheng et al., 2026;Sengupta and Wang, 2026;Sarafian et al., 2026;Karten et al., 2026;Lou et al., 2026;Zhang et al., 2026a). Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) and AHE (Lin et al., 2026) address automated harness evolution, which are closely related to our work. Meta-Harness searches harness programs using prior candidate code, scores, and execution traces. AHE exposes coding-agent harness components as editable files, organizes execution traces for analysis, and checks whether subsequent evaluation results match the expected effects of proposed changes. Both approaches support automated harness evolution and cross-model transfer. However, organizing optimization around programs or editable components does not by itself specify where an intervention belongs in the interaction loop or what responsibility it should carry. Concurrent work HarnessX (Chen et al., 2026) represents harnesses as typed, composable primitives and uses multi-agent analysis of execution traces to evolve their composition. LIFE-HARNESS instead organizes harness adaptation around four explicit roles in the interaction lifecycle: environment contracts before interaction, procedural skills during task conditioning, action realization before execution, and trajectory regulation after feedback. These roles map recurring failures to targeted edits. Prompt Adaptation Methods. Prompt optimizers rewrite instructions, demonstrations, or templates using feedback, including PromptWizard, OPRO, TextGrad, GEPA and ACE (Agarwal et al., 2024a;Yang et al., 2024a;Yuksekgonul et al., 2024;Agrawal et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2026b). LIFE-HARNESS extends adaptation beyond prompts to the broader runtime harness interface. Model-side Adaptation for LLM Agents. Instruction tuning, tool-use fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and distillation improve agents through parameter updates (Qwen Team et al., 2025;Prabhakar et al., 2025;Guo et al., 2025;Xu et al., 2026;Qian et al., 2025;Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). LIFE-HARNESS complements these approaches by adapting the runtime interface around existing model checkpoints while keeping their parameters fixed.

div.head: LLM Agents as Runtime Systems
div.p: An LLM agent is a policy π θ interacting with a stateful environment E, including a user U when applicable. An episode specifies a task x, an environment contract C, and a step budget B. The contract C defines tools, argument and feedback formats, answer formats, and task-specific policies.
Initialization yields (s 0 , o 0 ) = E.INIT(x). At step t, the interaction history is
The agent selects an action and receives environment feedback:
div.formula: a t ∼ π θ (• | τ t ), (s t+1 , o t+1 ) = E.STEP(s t , a t ).
div.p: Actions include tool calls, text commands, and final answers; text actions can be represented as pseudotools. The trajectory appends (a t , o t+1 ), including error feedback, until task completion, environment termination, or budget exhaustion.

div.head: Parameter vs. Runtime Interface Adaptation
div.p: Given training trajectories T train , conventional parameter adaptation updates model weights, whereas runtime interface adaptation updates the harness H while keeping θ fixed:
div.formula: θ ′ ← A param (θ, T train ), H ′ ← A harness (H, T train ).
div.p: Parameter adaptation embeds task-specific structure in model weights and is model-and taskspecific. Our complementary approach adapts how the model interacts with the environment without changing model weights or evaluation protocols.
It is environment-specific but model-agnostic: the adapted harness can be reused across model backbones following the same interaction protocol, without retraining.

div.head: Method: LIFE-HARNESS
div.p: We propose LIFE-HARNESS, an evolving lifecycle runtime harness for deterministic LLM agents. The harness adapts the model-environment interface rather than model weights. It operates on the interaction loop defined in Section 3.1: the environment contract C, the task description x, the environment state s t , the model action a t , and the trajectory τ t .

div.head: Failure Diagnosis
div.p: Before designing the harness, we first diagnose the primary failure modes of baseline agents. We evaluate a frozen Qwen3-4B-Instruct on training tasks across diverse interactive agent environments, and manually review LLM-generated failure annotations. For each failed episode, we assign a As shown in Figure 3, deterministic agent failures are heterogeneous: all four categories occur in practice, and the dominant mode varies substantially across environments. This motivates a harness with multiple intervention points, spanning environment-contract clarification, procedural retrieval, pre-execution action validation, and postexecution trajectory regulation.

div.head: Overview
div.p: Guided by the failure diagnosis above, LIFE-HARNESS comprises four layers integrated across different stages of the agent lifecycle. Figure 4 provides an overview of LIFE-HARNESS.

❶ Environment Contract Layer operates before interaction. It makes stable environment constraints explicit, including tool-use rules, policy constraints, and common pitfalls that agents frequently encounter in the target environment.

❷ Procedural Skill Layer operates at the taskconditioning stage. It maintains a skill library distilled from training trajectories and retrieves relevant skills based on the user's task description. ❸ Action Realization Layer operates after the model outputs an action and before the environment executes it. It verifies whether the action is executable under the environment contract, canonicalizes unambiguous interface-level errors, and blocks actions that would deterministically fail. This layer ensures that the model's intended operation is reliably mapped to a valid tool call or environment action.

❹ Trajectory Regulation Layer operates after environment feedback is returned. It monitors the updated trajectory for non-progressing patterns such as repetition, stagnation, or budget exhaustion, and triggers recovery when needed. This layer specifically targets trajectory degeneration.
Together, these layers adapt the runtime interface through which the model interacts with the environment. The model weights remain fixed, and the evaluation environment is unchanged.

div.head: Environment Contract Layer
div.p: This layer makes stable environment constraints explicit before interaction by adapting the modelvisible contract C. Formally, it produces an enhanced contract C ′ = C ⊕ ∆ C , where ∆ C contains concise updates derived from environment policies, API behavior, and recurring failures in training trajectories. The enhanced contract C ′ is shown to the model in place of C, enabling the agent to better utilize the given tools. In practice, ∆ C may specify how tools should be called, which actions are admissible under the environment protocol, and which environment-specific pitfalls should be avoided.

div.head: Procedural Skill Layer
div.p: This layer provides non-parametric guidance from training trajectories. A skill is a compact and reusable strategy that captures the essence of how to accomplish specific subtasks.
Let S be the skill memory constructed from training trajectories. For a task description x, the harness retrieves relevant skills:
div.formula: K x = TopK k∈S score(x, k),
div.p: where score is implemented with BM25 in our experiments. The retrieved skills K x are inserted into the initial system prompt to guide the model on how to solve specific common problems.

div.head: Action Realization Layer
div.p: This layer operates after the model outputs an action and before the environment executes it. Given the model action a t , the current trajectory τ t , and the current state s t , the layer either submits this action a t to the environment or returns a modelvisible block message m t :
div.formula: z t = REALIZEACTION(a t , τ t , s t ) z t ∈ {EXEC(a t ), BLOCK(m t )}.
div.p: It uses deterministic environment evidence, such as tool schemas, admissible action sets, argument constraints, and task policies, to enforce the prevention of erroneous tool calls at the execution level.

div.head: Trajectory Regulation Layer
div.p: The Trajectory Regulation Layer monitors the interaction after environment execution. Many agent failures are self-reinforcing: the agent repeats the same invalid command, loops between equivalent states, or exhausts the budget without making progress. div.head: Trajectory-Driven Harness Evolution
div.p: LIFE-HARNESS evolves its harness through a repeated cycle of trajectory collection, failure analysis, harness updates, and evaluation, as illustrated in Figure 4. Each round starts by running the frozen solver with the current harness on a batch of training tasks. The resulting trajectories show which actions the agent took, what feedback it received, and where progress broke down. An evolution LLM examines these trajectories alongside the current harness to identify recurring failures and propose targeted changes. Throughout evolution, the solver, environment, scoring rules, and interaction budgets remain fixed, and only training evidence is used.

The four layers guide these changes. Misunderstood tool-use rules motivate updates to the Environment Contract Layer; ineffective subtask strategies motivate reusable guidance in the Procedural Skill Layer; malformed or inadmissible actions motivate checks in the Action Realization Layer; and repeated actions or stalled progress motivate recovery interventions in the Trajectory Regulation Layer. The evolution LLM can add, revise, or remove mechanisms within these layers.

Evaluation then determines whether to retain the updated harness in two stages. First, interface checks and replay on training traces test execution validity; failed checks are returned to the evolution LLM for up to three repair attempts. A valid candidate is then evaluated against the current harness on the same training batch using the benchmark's native scorer. It replaces the current harness only if accuracy improves. Otherwise, the current harness is retained, and the next round uses a new training batch to expose additional failure patterns. After evolution, the retained harness is frozen for heldout evaluation. Appendix A.2 provides the detailed protocol and prompt template.

div.head: Experimental Setup
div.p: Benchmarks. We evaluate LIFE-HARNESS on four benchmark suites: τ -bench (Yao et al., 2024), τ 2 -bench (Barres et al., 2025), AgentBench (Liu et al., 2024), and AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), covering eight agent environments: Airline, Retail, Telecom, ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020), WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), OS, DBBench, and AppWorld.

Baselines. We compare LIFE-HARNESS with Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026), AHE (Lin et al., 2026), ALIGN (Liu et al., 2025), and AgentSquare (Shang et al., 2025). For Meta-Harness and AHE, we run harness evolution using open-source implementations under the same conditions as LIFE-HARNESS, including the solver, evolution LLM, and rollout and evaluation settings. Three methods undergo six evolution rounds using identical training batches of up to 50 tasks per round. For ALIGN and AgentSquare, we evaluate their released final harnesses on ALFWorld and WebShop. Models. Throughout harness evolution, we use Qwen3-4B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025) as the frozen solver and GPT-5.5 as the evolution LLM. Held-out test data are excluded from evolution. The selected harness is frozen and reused to evaluate 17 additional open-weight model backbones, spanning Qwen (Qwen Team et al., 2025;Qwen Team, 2025, 2026), Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and xLAM (Prabhakar et al., 2025) families, including instruction-tuned, reasoning, and agent-specialized models. We also evaluate GPT 5.5, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.1 Pro on the seven AgentBench and τ environments using the same frozen harnesses. Evaluation Parameters. div.head: Limitations
div.p: Our evaluation covers text-and API-based agent environments. We leave the evaluation of LIFE-HARNESS on visual GUI tasks, such as desktop and mobile application operation, to future work. These settings would extend the empirical scope of runtime harness adaptation to agents that interact through visual observations and graphical actions.

div.head: A Detailed Harness
div.p: A.1 Failure Annotation Protocol

We use an LLM to annotate failed trajectories, and human reviewers check all annotations. For each failed episode, the LLM reads the complete interaction trace and assigns one primary failure category according to the rule-based protocol below. The classification is performed trajectory by trajectory, rather than from aggregate statistics. We use a priority-based protocol: the annotator first checks for action realization failures, then environment contract mismatches, then trajectory degeneration, and finally assigns the episode to the residual category. This priority order prevents later symptoms from hiding earlier interface failures. For example, if an agent writes a tool call in plain text, the environment never executes it, and the episode eventually exhausts the step budget, we annotate it as an action realization failure rather than trajectory degeneration.
Action realization failures. This category corresponds to failures targeted by the Action Realization Layer. A failed episode is assigned to this category if any of the following conditions hold:

• The assistant does not produce executable tool_calls, but instead writes in content an action or answer that should have been submitted through a tool, such as take_action({...}), answer_action({...}), a natural-language command, SQL text, or the final answer text.
• The assistant produces a tool call, but the call cannot be executed because of an invalid function name, JSON parsing failure, missing required arguments, or incorrect argument types.

• In DBBench, the SQL query is not executable due to interface, dialect, or formatting violations, such as unquoted column names containing spaces, malformed table names, or invalid concatenation syntax.
The key criterion is that the model's intent may be reasonable, but it is not submitted in a form executable by the environment.

Environment contract mismatches. This category corresponds to failures targeted by the Environment Contract Layer. It is considered only when the action interface is executable. A failed episode is assigned to this category if any of the following conditions hold:
• The agent uses the wrong tool for a critical step, such as calling a finish tool when an answer-submission tool is required.

• The tool choice or calling order violates the task protocol, such as submitting prematurely, skipping a required intermediate tool, or using a search tool to encode constraints that should not be searched directly.

• The argument has an incorrect semantic format, although it satisfies the JSON or schemalevel interface. For example, in DBBench, the final answer may be required to be an exact value or list, but the agent submits a naturallanguage explanation, or multi-column results are concatenated into free-form text instead of the required format.
The key criterion is that the function call is structurally present and executable, but the agent misunderstands the tool's purpose, boundary, calling protocol, or argument semantics.

Trajectory degeneration. This category corresponds to failures targeted by the Trajectory Regulation Layer. It is considered only when neither action realization nor environment contract mismatch is the primary cause. A failed episode is assigned to this category if any of the following conditions hold:

• The episode ends due to task limit reached or an equivalent budget-exhaustion signal, and the trajectory contains a clear repetition pattern, such as repeatedly issuing the same action, oscillating between two states, repeatedly calling look, inventory, or examine, repeatedly searching or clicking, or repeatedly returning to the same page.

• The agent commits to an incorrect strategy early and reinforces it throughout the trajectory, such as searching once and purchasing without comparing candidates or required attributes, or repeatedly visiting already explored locations after failing to find the target.
• The environment repeatedly returns noprogress feedback, such as Nothing happens or an unchanged page/state over many steps.
The key criterion is that individual actions are usually executable, but the long-horizon interaction fails to use environment feedback to revise the strategy.

div.head: Residual reasoning failures.
div.p: A failed episode is assigned to this category when none of the above categories apply. This category includes cases where the tool-use protocol is largely followed, but the agent makes an incorrect reasoning, computation, SQL, retrieval, or value-selection decision. It also includes cases where the agent retrieves the wrong object or answer for reasons not attributable to tool-protocol misunderstanding or trajectory loops, or where the correct task path is attempted but the final value, condition, or filtering logic is wrong.

div.head: A.2 Harness Evolution Protocol and Prompt
div.p: The two templates below summarize the core prompts used for harness evolution and validation repair in Section 4.4. The evolution prompt combines fixed instructions with round-specific inputs; the repair prompt supplies validation feedback within the same proposal. Inspect relevant evidence on demand, implement a candidate update, and submit it for evaluation after validation.

div.head: Validation Repair Prompt
div.p: Candidate validation failed. This is repair attempt {attempt} of 3 for the same proposal. Validation feedback: {validation_errors}. Inspect the reported defects, revise the candidate, and rerun validation. Keep the original optimization boundaries unchanged. This repair attempt does not impose a limit on evidence reads or interaction turns. Successful validation permits task-accuracy evaluation; it does not establish an accuracy gain.
